Markov random field lattice
Click any white x node to show its local Markov blanket.

plan.contextChunk: This figure is a line drawing of a graphical model laid out as a two-dimensional lattice in oblique projection, built from two kinds of nodes. Open white circles occupy the lattice sites, arranged in three receding rows of three visible sites each; within a row they are joined by horizontal edges that run past the rightmost circle to the frame edge, and between rows by short diagonal edges slanting down and to the left, which likewise continue off the lower-left corner, so the grid reads as a fragment of an unbounded array. A single vertical edge rises from each white circle to a solid gray filled circle, one gray node per site, drawn above and slightly behind its partner. Only the back row carries labels: its white circles are marked with the boldface symbols x_1, x_2, and x_3, and the gray circles directly above them y_1, y_2, and y_3. Because every gray node hangs off exactly one white node while the white nodes alone form the grid, the drawing separates per-site attachments from neighbor-to-neighbor coupling. The structure depicts a Markov random field over a spatial grid, each site carrying a state variable tied to its four lattice neighbors.

elements: nine open white circular hidden-state nodes x arranged as a 3 by 3 oblique lattice fragment
three back-row white nodes labeled x_1, x_2, and x_3
nine filled gray circular observation nodes y, one directly above each white x node
three back-row gray nodes labeled y_1, y_2, and y_3
black horizontal hidden-state grid edges connecting neighboring x nodes within each of the three rows
rightward horizontal continuation stubs extending beyond the rightmost x node in each row
black diagonal hidden-state grid edges connecting neighboring x nodes between adjacent receding rows
lower-left diagonal continuation stubs extending beyond the front/lower-left boundary of the lattice fragment
black vertical observation-link edges from each x node to its corresponding gray y node
thick black circular outlines around all white and gray nodes
large serif math labels with subscripts for x_1, x_2, x_3, y_1, y_2, and y_3

interactions.teaches: A hidden variable in the Markov random field is conditionally tied to its four neighboring hidden variables and to its own local observation, while distant nodes matter only through paths across the lattice

interactions.label: Model view
interactions.teaches: Separates the two kinds of structure: neighbor coupling among hidden x variables versus one-to-one evidence links from observations y to hidden states

interactions.label: Neighbor coupling strength
interactions.teaches: Stronger pairwise coupling makes adjacent hidden variables prefer similar values, producing a smoother spatial field while the observation nodes remain fixed

demo_steps.title: Full graphical model
demo_steps.narration: The full view shows both parts of the model: white hidden variables form a coupled lattice, and each gray observation variable attaches to exactly one hidden variable.

demo_steps.title: Hidden-state lattice only
demo_steps.narration: Hide the gray observation links to focus on the Markov random field itself. The white x nodes are coupled only to their nearest lattice neighbors.

demo_steps.title: Observation attachments only
demo_steps.narration: Hide the horizontal and diagonal x-x edges to see that each y node provides local evidence for just one corresponding x node.

demo_steps.title: Increase spatial coupling
demo_steps.narration: With stronger coupling, the white x nodes acquire more similar grayscale values across neighboring sites. This illustrates how pairwise potentials encourage spatial smoothness.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use an oblique layout with +X drawn horizontally screen-right, +Y drawn vertically screen-up, and +Z drawn as the receding diagonal down-left at roughly 55 degrees from the +X screen direction. The hidden lattice is a 3 by 3 fragment in the X-Z plane at Y=0. Let columns c=0,1,2 have X positions 0, 2.4, 4.8 world units. Let rows r=0,1,2 have Z positions 0, 2.1, 4.2 world units, where r=0 is the back/top row carrying the labels x_1, x_2, x_3 and y_1, y_2, y_3; increasing Z shifts the row down-left on screen. All x nodes are circles/discs of radius 0.36 world units centered at (X=2.4c, Y=0, Z=2.1r). All y nodes are same-radius gray circles centered directly above their partner at (X=2.4c, Y=1.75, Z=2.1r), so the x-y attachment is a vertical screen line. Hidden x-x row edges run horizontally along +X between adjacent columns for each row, with additional rightward continuation stubs of about 1.6 units beyond c=2; include short leftward continuation where visible only if it does not clutter the crop. Hidden x-x inter-row edges run along +Z between adjacent rows at each column, appearing as black diagonals slanting down-left; continue these diagonals about 1.6 units past the lower-left/front boundary to imply the infinite lattice. Edge stroke color black #000000, stroke width about 0.055 world units or 3 screen pixels. x node fill is white #ffffff with black outline #000000, outline width about 0.06 world units. y node fill is medium gray #8f8f8f with black outline. Labels are black serif italic/math text, large relative to the nodes: x_i labels sit immediately upper-right of the back-row white circles, partially overlapping the vertical stem region as in the source; y_i labels sit above and slightly right of the corresponding gray circles. For the coupling slider, use a fixed illustrative 3 by 3 evidence pattern over the x sites, for example e = [[0.15, 0.85, 0.30], [0.75, 0.25, 0.65], [0.20, 0.70, 0.40]] ordered by rows r=0..2 and columns c=0..2. Convert coupling beta to displayed hidden intensities by smoothing with x(beta) = inverse(I + beta*L) e, where L is the 4-neighbor graph Laplacian on the visible grid with implied Neumann boundary behavior. Map low values to white/light gray and high values to darker gray, but keep outlines black and keep all y nodes fixed at #8f8f8f. At beta=0 in the initial source-like view, x nodes may remain pure white until the learner moves the slider, preserving the textbook drawing.
interactionPlan.notes: Render this as a clean line drawing rather than a shaded 3D solid scene. Use an orthographic camera plus an oblique projection/shear or manually project world coordinates to screen so circles remain true circles like the source. Draw all edges first, then draw circular node discs above the edges to mask line intersections inside nodes. The view toggle should show/hide edge groups: Hidden-state lattice shows x nodes plus horizontal/diagonal x-x edges and x labels; Observation attachments shows x nodes, y nodes, vertical x-y links, and both x/y labels but hides x-x edges; Full model shows all groups. On click, highlight the selected x node with a blue outline, its visible four-neighbor x nodes with pale yellow fill or yellow halo, and its attached y node with an orange halo; fade all unrelated edges and nodes to about 15-25% opacity. For boundary x nodes, indicate off-frame missing neighbors with small dashed ghost markers or highlighted continuation stubs so the learner still sees the intended four-neighbor Markov blanket of the unbounded lattice.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Click any white x node to highlight its four neighboring x nodes and its attached gray y node; all other edges fade, making the local Markov blanket and conditional dependence structure visible.
- Toggle between hidden-state lattice, observation attachments, and full model views; white grid edges, gray vertical links, or both appear in turn, separating neighbor coupling from per-site evidence.
- Slider for coupling strength between neighboring x nodes; neighboring white nodes gradually take on similar shading while y nodes remain fixed, showing how pairwise potentials encourage spatial smoothness across the field.

authoredContext:
To capture relationships over space, a two-dimensional (2D) structure is
useful, called a Markov random field (MRF):

Two-dimensional Markov random field.

An example of how Markov random field models are applied to images is
depicted in the figure, which show a small image region and its context
in the image (the figure [a]). The figure [b] shows an MRF with each
node corresponding to a pixel of the image region. The states of an MRF
can be indicator variables of image segment membership for each pixel.
The states of a hypothetical most-probable configuration of this MRF are
shown as the color of each node in this illustration.

Fig (a) Image to be segmented and a local region of (a) marked in red. (b) Visualization of an MRF of nodes corresponding to image pixels inside the marked region, with states indicating segment membership, for a hypothetical most probable configuration.

discrepancies: The generated lattice is much smaller within the canvas and has more surrounding whitespace than the tightly cropped source figure.
The x labels are placed too close to adjacent gray observation nodes, with x1 and x2 visually overlapping nearby circles more than in the source.
Some continuation stubs at the lattice boundaries are shorter and less prominent than the long off-frame lines in the source.
The generated figure adds a large explanatory control panel and interactive Markov-blanket/coupling features that are not visually present in the original static figure.
evaluation.notes: The generated figure is clearly recognizable as the same hidden-observation lattice, with correct node colors and connections, but label placement and boundary line proportions are less faithful.
action_items: Move the x1, x2, and x3 labels slightly farther right/up so they do not overlap neighboring gray observation circles.
Increase the rendered lattice scale or adjust the initial camera framing so the diagram fills the canvas more like the source.
Lengthen the rightward and lower diagonal continuation edges to better match the source's off-frame lattice continuation.
Keep optional interaction highlights visually inactive by default so the static view remains as close as possible to the source.
